Return a complete version 2b1 ordered block envelope using the supplied JSON schema. Use text blocks for prose. At most one ui block contains only the requested protocol source and initial integer state entries (empty uses defaults). No fences. No JavaScript, tools, events, HTML or links. One Stack with unique named leaves. Up to 40 leaves, 40 collection members, 64 declarations, depth 32, 16000 UTF-8 source bytes, 10000 frame bytes. Integers for input state. Names start with ASCII letter, then alphanumeric or underscore, at most 48 characters. All declarations must be reachable. Text and labels at most 512 characters. Safe Graphic items use kind plus only required fields: rect(x,y,width,height), circle(cx,cy,r), text(x,y,text), path(d using only M L H V Z, lowercase equivalents, numbers, spaces or commas), group(items of leaves). Numeric coordinates 0..640; viewBox 0 0 450 135.
One assignment per physical line. root = Stack([leafName, otherLeaf]). Each leaf is one named call: Text("text"), Metric("label",numericValue), Control("label",literalMin,literalMax,choices,$variable), Table([{label:"name",score:number}]), Graphic("label",items). Declare $variable = integer and bind it to exactly one Control. Use [] for range or literal string options indexed 0..n-1. Derived name = expression. Strings use double quotes. Numeric + - * /, == > <, condition ? yes : no, arrays, objects, named references, @Sum(numbers), @Sort(rows,"score","desc") are allowed. No unary minus, concatenation, member access, map, interpolation or inline nested components. Produce complete root and definitions.
Choose text for a simple definition. Use a legible diagram if spatial relationships aid understanding. Use controls for a changing decision. Label units, state assumptions, use short readable labels, give each output an informative name and check zero or boundary conditions. Keep geometry inside the viewBox.
Treat the request as the complete source of domain rules. Include exactly its input dimensions, options, units, defaults and ranges. Check that each input changes the intended outputs. Do not invent extra tiers, exceptions or fees. Interpret terminology in its application context. Provide an actual interaction when requested. Do not claim a visible control exists in prose alone.
Explain the geometric meaning of a vector dot product, including orthogonal vectors and negative projection.

{"version":"2b1","blocks":[{"type":"text","text":"The dot product of two vectors is a scalar that measures how much one vector extends in the direction of another. Geometrically, it equals the product of their lengths and the cosine of the angle between them."},{"type":"ui","source":"protocol Source
integer angleDegrees = 45  // Angle between vectors in degrees, from 0 to 180
end
","state":[{"name":"angleDegrees","value":45}]},{"type":"text","text":"If \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) are vectors with lengths \(|\mathbf{a}|\) and \(|\mathbf{b}|\), and \(\theta\) is the angle between them, then:
\[ \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}| \times |\mathbf{b}| \times \cos(\theta) \]
This means:"},{"type":"text","text":"- When \(\theta = 0^\circ\), vectors point the same way, and the dot product is positive and maximal.
- When \(\theta = 90^\circ\), vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular), and the dot product is zero.
- When \(\theta > 90^\circ\), the dot product is negative, indicating the projection of one vector onto the other points opposite to the vector's direction."},{"type":"text","text":"The dot product also represents the length of the projection of one vector onto another, multiplied by the length of the vector being projected onto. This projection can be positive, zero, or negative depending on the angle."},{"type":"ui","source":"protocol Source
integer lengthA = 100  // Length of vector a
integer lengthB = 80   // Length of vector b
end
","state":[{"name":"lengthA","value":100},{"name":"lengthB","value":80}]},{"type":"text","text":"Using the inputs, the dot product is computed as:
\[ \text{DotProduct} = lengthA \times lengthB \times \cos(angleDegrees \times \pi / 180) \]"},{"type":"text","text":"Below is a diagram illustrating vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) with angle \(\theta\) between them, their projection, and the meaning of the dot product."}

{"version":"2b1","blocks":[{"type":"text","text":"The dot product of two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is a scalar value representing how much one vector extends in the direction of the other. Geometrically, it equals the product of their lengths and the cosine of the angle \(\theta\) between them."},{"type":"ui","source":"protocol Source
integer angleDegrees = 45  // Angle between vectors in degrees, range 0 to 180
integer lengthA = 100      // Length of vector a, range 0 to 200
integer lengthB = 80       // Length of vector b, range 0 to 200
end
","state":[{"name":"angleDegrees","value":45},{"name":"lengthA","value":100},{"name":"lengthB","value":80}]},{"type":"text","text":"Mathematically, the dot product is:
\[ \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}| \times |\mathbf{b}| \times \cos(\theta) \]
where \(|\mathbf{a}|\) and \(|\mathbf{b}|\) are the lengths of vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\theta\) is the angle between them in degrees."},{"type":"text","text":"Interpretation of the dot product based on \(\theta\):
- \(\theta = 0^\circ\): vectors point in the same direction; dot product is positive and maximal.
- \(\theta = 90^\circ\): vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular); dot product is zero.
- \(90^\circ < \theta \leq 180^\circ\): dot product is negative, indicating the projection of one vector onto the other is opposite in direction."},{"type":"text","text":"The dot product also equals the length of \(\mathbf{a}\) multiplied by the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{b}\) onto \(\mathbf{a}\). This scalar projection can be positive, zero, or negative depending on the angle."},{"type":"text","text":"Using the inputs, the dot product is computed as:
\[ \text{DotProduct} = lengthA \times lengthB \times \cos(angleDegrees \times \pi / 180) \]"},{"type":"text","text":"Below is a diagram illustrating vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), the angle \(\theta\) between them, and the projection of \(\mathbf{b}\) onto \(\mathbf{a}\). The projection length corresponds to \( |\mathbf{b}| \cos(\theta) \), which multiplied by \( |\mathbf{a}| \) gives the dot product."},{"type":"ui","source":"protocol Source
end
","state":[]}] }
